quizzes.stem: A team lead wants an assistant to prepare a weekly status email from a spreadsheet of task progress notes. The email goes to executives. Which division of work is soundest?

options.a: Claude writes the first version; a person verifies facts and approves sending
options.b: A person writes the email; Claude only corrects spelling and grammar
options.c: Claude drafts and also decides which blockers to escalate to executives
options.d: Claude collects the notes, writes the email and sends it, with spot checks later

explanation.a: Drafting is language-shaped and reviewable, while checking facts and approving the send stay with a person (the worked example's table).
explanation.d: Ruled out because the table keeps "Check every figure in the draft against the source" with a person or a script, and spot checks later come after readers have the email.
explanation.b: Ruled out because Claude "saves the time spent on prose", the main saving, which a person writing everything forgoes.
explanation.c: Ruled out because escalation is "judgment that carries accountability", which stays with a person.

quizzes.stem: Someone asks Claude: "Summarise this report." The result is accurate, but the sales team who asked cannot use it. Which gap in the request most likely caused this?

options.a: It lacked a role line naming Claude an expert summariser
options.b: It set no word limit, so Claude could not tell which points to cut
options.c: It never said who would read it or what they must decide with it
options.d: It ran on a tier too small to judge what matters to sales

explanation.c: The description should cover the goal and the context, who reads it and why, and a generic request gets a generic reply.
explanation.a: Ruled out because what is missing is the goal and "the context (who reads it, what happened before)", and a role line supplies neither.
explanation.b: Ruled out because without the goal "Claude cannot choose between reasonable readings", so a limit forces cuts without saying which points matter to sales.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "the description is where most of the quality is decided", and a larger tier does not know the readers either.

quizzes.stem: An analyst asks Claude to summarise a regulation for compliance colleagues. The summary cites "subsection 14(b)(ii)" for a retention rule, and the analyst is about to forward it. What is the most appropriate step?

options.a: Ask Claude whether it is confident, and forward the summary if it says yes
options.b: Find that clause in the official text and read what it says before sending
options.c: Ask Claude to cite the subsection again in a fresh reply and compare the two
options.d: Forward it with a note that an AI drafted it, so readers can judge

explanation.b: Specific citations are the kind of detail a model can invent, so the claim that would hurt if wrong is checked against the source of record (the checking routine).
explanation.a: Ruled out because the routine says that asking the model how sure it is, or "for its confidence does not verify anything".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the routine says to check "against the source of record, not against the model", and a second reply from the same model is not the source.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it", so a note about the AI's part hands the check to readers and leaves the unverified citation still the analyst's to fix.

quizzes.stem: A competitor table has one cell marked "data unavailable" while every other cell is filled. A colleague asks you to drop that row so the table looks finished. Which response is best?

options.a: Ask Claude to try again until every cell holds a value
options.b: Fill it with a typical industry figure and label it an estimate
options.c: Show a dash in that cell and drop any mention of the missing data
options.d: Retain the entry as it stands and state what could not be located

explanation.d: A declared gap is information, and the careful move is to keep it and decide what to do (the spotting a gap section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex", and pressing for a value invites invention.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "the careless move is to fill the gap with an estimate".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the page says "Keep the gap and decide what to do about it", not hide it behind a dash.

quizzes.stem: A team uses Claude to draft a monthly variance narrative from a finance export. After a few clean months the lead proposes two changes: Claude will also decide which variances reach the directors, and the figure-by-figure review stops. Which response applies both pages?

options.a: Keep the judgment call with a person and keep verifying every number against its source
options.b: Let Claude take the judgment call, since clean drafts show sound judgment, and keep verifying numbers
options.c: Drop the verification, since clean drafts show the numbers are right, and keep the judgment call human
options.d: Let Claude take both, and ask it to flag any figure it doubts

explanation.a: Judgment that carries accountability stays with a person, and figures are checked against the source of record however clean past drafts were (page 1 delegation table; page 2 checking routine).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table gives "Decide which variances matter to the board" to a person, as judgment with accountability, and a clean run does not move it.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "A good draft does not show the figures were right", so a run of clean drafts is no reason to stop verifying.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy", and a flag from the model replaces neither the person nor the check.

quizzes.stem: A support lead gets a drafted reply to an angry customer that is accurate but reads like a legal notice. The lead needs the next attempt to come out right. What should the lead do next?

options.a: Add a rule that the reply must stay under a hundred words
options.b: Run the same request again and keep the reply that sounds friendliest
options.c: Add a short example message in the voice that suits an upset person
options.d: Rewrite the role, length, tone and format lines together in one go

explanation.c: What is wrong is the voice, so the one change aimed at it is a sample of the style wanted, which page 1 lists for drafting, and revising the request rather than re-running it is the method (page 1, describe; page 2, iterate).
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex", and picking the friendliest of several runs leaves the request as loose as before.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "drafting wants audience, tone and an example", and a word count gives none of the three, so a shorter reply can still read like a legal notice.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the method is to "change one thing in the description" and then "compare the result with the last", and rewriting four lines at once hides which one fixed the voice.

quizzes.stem: A consultant forwards a client a report that Claude drafted. The client later finds a wrong number in it. Who answers for the mistake, and what should have happened first?

options.a: The tool's provider owns it, and the sender should have asked it to double-check
options.b: The sender owns it, and should have checked each figure against its source
options.c: The recipient owns it, and should have queried the number before relying on it
options.d: The sender owns it, and should have checked that the tone suited the client

explanation.b: The sender owns what was sent, and figures are checked against the source of record before release (page 2, take responsibility and the checking routine; page 1, where checking every figure sits with a person or a script).
explanation.a: Ruled out because "You own what you send, whoever drafted it", and asking the tool to recheck its own number is no check, since asking it "for its confidence does not verify anything".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "the person who relied on it will not distinguish between you and the tool", so blame does not move to the reader.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible, and skip figures and citations", and a tone check would have left the wrong number in the report.

quizzes.stem: A team asks Claude to fill a supplier price table from a PDF. Every row comes back filled, including one cost the PDF never states, and the table goes to the finance director today. Which pair of actions fits both pages?

options.a: Proofread the labels and layout, then send the table as filled
options.b: Ask for a confidence beside each entry, then keep the entries marked high
options.c: Run the same extraction twice more, then keep the cost that all three runs return
options.d: Have it mark any value it cannot find as missing, then check the rest at source

explanation.d:
Page 1 puts the rule in the description ("say so rather than estimating"), page 2 says a declared gap is
   information to keep, and the figures that remain are checked against the source of record.
explanation.a:
is ruled out
   because "Readers check tone and grammar, which are visible, and skip figures and citations", which is where the
   damage is.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".
explanation.c:
is ruled out
   because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex", and runs that agree on a cost the PDF never
   states are the model agreeing with itself, not a check "against the source of record".
